slides.title: Normalization in Database Design
slides.subtitle: Eliminating redundancy through functional dependencies
agenda: BCNF and trade-offs in real systems
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome. Today we explore normalization—a formal method for structuring relational databases to prevent redundancy and update anomalies. We’ll build from functional dependencies up to BCNF, using concrete examples from real systems. By the end, you’ll be able to decompose schemas, identify violations, and evaluate when denormalization is justified—especially in ML pipelines where data consistency is critical.

slides.title: Functional Dependencies Define Semantic Constraints
bullets: A functional dependency $ X \rightarrow Y $ means identical X-values imply identical Y-values in all valid instances
FDs are domain-driven constraints, not data observations—e.g., $ \text{StudentID} \rightarrow \text{Email} $ by policy
Attribute closure $ X^+ $ computes all attributes determined by X using Armstrong’s axioms
Closure identifies superkeys: if $ X^+ $ includes all attributes, X is a superkey
Candidate keys are minimal superkeys—no subset is also a superkey
slides.speaker_notes: Functional dependencies are the grammar of relational design. They encode business rules—like 'each student has one email'—that must hold across time and data. Attribute closure lets us reason about what a set of attributes can determine. This is essential for identifying keys and detecting redundancy. Remember: normalization depends on *all* candidate keys, not just the primary key chosen in implementation.

slides.title: Attribute Closure Uses Functional Dependencies
slides.equation_tex: X^+ = \bigcup \{ A \mid X \rightarrow A \text{ is implied by } F \}
slides.equation_caption: The closure of X is the set of all attributes A logically implied by the FD set F.
bullets: Start with X, repeatedly apply FDs to add determined attributes
Stop when no new attributes can be added
Used to test superkeys: if $ X^+ = R $, then X is a superkey
Also verifies if an FD $ X \rightarrow Y $ is implied by a given set
slides.speaker_notes: Closure is the engine of normalization analysis. You begin with a set of attributes and apply known FDs iteratively until no more attributes can be derived. This process answers: 'If I know these values, what else must I know?' In practice, it’s how we prove that a set is a candidate key or detect hidden dependencies that could cause anomalies later.

slides.title: Find Candidate Keys Using Closure
slides.exercise_prompt: Given relation $ R(\text{StudentID}, \text{Email}, \text{Course}, \text{Grade}) $ with FDs: $ \text{StudentID} \rightarrow \text{Email} $, $ \{\text{StudentID}, \text{Course}\} \rightarrow \text{Grade} $, $ \text{Email} \rightarrow \text{StudentID} $. Compute closures for $ \{\text{StudentID}, \text{Course}\} $ and $ \{\text{Email}, \text{Course}\} $. Are both candidate keys? Justify minimality.
bullets: Hint: Apply FDs step-by-step to grow the closure
Check minimality by removing one attribute and recomputing
Recall: a candidate key must be a minimal superkey
slides.speaker_notes: Take five minutes to work through this. Start with $ \{\text{StudentID}, \text{Course}\} $: apply $ \text{StudentID} \rightarrow \text{Email} $, then $ \{\text{StudentID}, \text{Course}\} \rightarrow \text{Grade} $. You’ll cover all attributes. Now test subsets—removing either breaks closure. Repeat for $ \{\text{Email}, \text{Course}\} $. The result? Two candidate keys. This shows why we must consider all keys, not just one designated primary key.

slides.title: 1NF Requires Atomic Attribute Values
bullets: A relation is in 1NF if all attributes are atomic and tuples are unique
Multivalued fields like comma-separated lists violate 1NF
Non-atomic values prevent indexing, constraints, and reliable querying
Normalization splits multivalued attributes into separate rows
Example: split {StudentID: 101, Courses: 'Math,Physics'} into three rows
slides.speaker_notes: First Normal Form is the bedrock. Without it, you can’t enforce constraints or query reliably. A field like 'Math,Physics,CS' is a string—not a set. The DBMS can’t understand its internal structure. By splitting into atomic tuples, we make each fact individually addressable. This is analogous to tokenizing text in NLP: you can’t analyze sentences without first splitting words.

slides.title: 2NF Eliminates Partial Dependencies on Composite Keys
bullets: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the full candidate key
Partial dependencies occur when a non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key
Example: $ \text{LibrarianOnDuty} \rightarrow \text{LibraryBranch} $ in a borrowing record
Decompose by moving the dependent attribute to a new table with its determinant
Result: $ \text{BORROWING} $ and $ \text{STAFF\_BRANCH}(\text{LibrarianOnDuty}, \text{LibraryBranch}) $
slides.speaker_notes: Second Normal Form targets redundancy from partial dependencies. If a non-key attribute doesn't need the full key, it doesn't belong in that table. In the library example, the branch is determined by the librarian, not the borrowing event. Leaving it in creates redundancy: every time a librarian appears, their branch is repeated. Decomposition removes this by isolating the dependency.

slides.title: Apply 2NF to a Composite Key Schema
slides.exercise_prompt: Given $ R(A,B,C,D) $ with candidate key $ \{A,B\} $, and FDs: $ A \rightarrow C $, $ B \rightarrow D $. Is R in 2NF? If not, decompose it into 2NF. Show the resulting relations and justify each step using functional dependencies.
bullets: Hint: Check if C depends fully on $ \{A,B\} $ or only on A
Identify partial dependencies and extract them into new relations
Ensure the decomposition preserves information and dependencies
slides.speaker_notes: Work through this step-by-step. $ C $ depends only on $ A $, which is part of the key—this is a partial dependency. Similarly, $ D $ depends only on $ B $. So $ R $ is not in 2NF. Decompose into $ R1(A,C) $, $ R2(B,D) $, and $ R3(A,B) $ to preserve the key. This eliminates redundancy while maintaining all original information.

slides.title: 3NF Removes Transitive Dependencies
bullets: A relation is in 3NF if every FD $ X \rightarrow Y $ has X as a superkey or Y as a prime attribute
This prevents non-key attributes from being determined by other non-key attributes
Transitive dependency example: $ \text{LibrarianOnDuty} \rightarrow \text{LibraryBranch} \rightarrow \text{City} $
Decompose into $ \text{STAFF}(\text{LibrarianOnDuty}, \text{LibraryBranch}) $ and $ \text{BRANCH}(\text{LibraryBranch}, \text{City}) $
3NF ensures derived data like City is updated in one place
slides.speaker_notes: Third Normal Form cuts indirect dependencies. If City depends on LibraryBranch, and LibraryBranch depends on Librarian, then City transitively depends on Librarian—but that’s fragile. If the branch moves, you must update every staff record. 3NF isolates the branch-city link so updates happen once. This is crucial in ML: if you embed derived features like City in logs, they become stale when source data changes.

slides.title: 3NF Condition: Superkey or Prime Attribute
slides.equation_tex: \text{For every } X \rightarrow Y, \text{ either } X \text{ is a superkey or } Y \subseteq \text{prime attributes}
slides.equation_caption: In 3NF, non-key attributes can only depend on keys, not on other non-key attributes.
bullets: Prime attributes are those part of any candidate key
This allows some non-superkey determinants if the dependent is prime
3NF permits limited redundancy to preserve dependencies
It is less strict than BCNF but often sufficient in practice
slides.speaker_notes: This equation defines 3NF precisely. It allows a functional dependency if either the determinant is a superkey—or the dependent attribute is prime, meaning it's part of some candidate key. This exception makes 3NF more flexible than BCNF. For example, if an FD like $ C \rightarrow B $ holds and B is in a key, it's allowed even if C isn't a superkey. This helps avoid losing dependencies during decomposition.

slides.title: BCNF Eliminates All FD-Based Redundancy
bullets: A relation is in BCNF if every non-trivial FD $ X \rightarrow Y $ has X as a superkey
BCNF is stricter than 3NF: it disallows even prime attribute dependencies from non-superkeys
Example: $ C \rightarrow B $ violates BCNF if C is not a superkey
Decomposition on $ C \rightarrow B $ yields $ R1(C,B) $ and $ R2(A,C) $
BCNF ensures every determinant is a key—clean, but may not preserve all FDs
slides.speaker_notes: Boyce-Codd Normal Form is the gold standard. It demands that *only* superkeys can determine other attributes. This eliminates all redundancy due to functional dependencies. But there's a cost: you may not be able to preserve all FDs after decomposition. The $ A \rightarrow B $, $ B \rightarrow C $, $ C \rightarrow A $ cycle shows this tension. BCNF prioritizes consistency over dependency preservation.

slides.title: Denormalization Requires Controlled Trade-Offs
bullets: OLTP systems favor normalization for consistency and update safety
OLAP and ML systems may denormalize for query performance
Denormalization should be based on a normalized source of truth
Use materialized views or caches with refresh guarantees
Example: store Age in ratings table only if synchronized from BirthDate
slides.speaker_notes: Normalization isn't dogma. In analytics and ML, joins can be expensive. Denormalizing—like embedding City in user logs—can speed up queries. But it must be done carefully. The normalized schema remains the source of truth. Denormalized data should be treated as a cache, updated consistently. Otherwise, you risk stale or contradictory features in training data.

slides.title: Decompose into BCNF with Dependency Analysis
slides.exercise_prompt: Given $ R(A,B,C) $ with FDs: $ AB \rightarrow C $, $ C \rightarrow B $. Find all candidate keys. Is R in 3NF? In BCNF? If not, decompose into BCNF. Does the decomposition preserve all FDs? Justify your answer.
bullets: Hint: Compute $ \{A,C\}^+ $ to test if it’s a key
Check if $ C \rightarrow B $ violates BCNF by testing if C is a superkey
After decomposition, verify whether $ AB \rightarrow C $ is still enforced
slides.speaker_notes: This exercise tests deep understanding. First, $ AB \rightarrow C $, and $ C \rightarrow B $ implies $ AC \rightarrow AB \rightarrow C $, so $ \{A,C\} $ is a key. $ C \rightarrow B $: C determines B, but C doesn’t determine A, so not a superkey. Thus, not in BCNF. Decompose into $ R1(C,B) $ and $ R2(A,C) $. But now $ AB \rightarrow C $ spans tables and isn’t preserved. This illustrates the dependency preservation trade-off inherent in BCNF.

slides.title: Normalization as a Design Lens, Not Just a Checklist
bullets: Normalization forces explicit modeling of what determines what
It prevents anomalies: update, delete, and insertion errors
Like type checking, it catches design flaws early
In ML pipelines, it ensures feature consistency over time
Use it iteratively—especially when adding new attributes or dependencies
slides.speaker_notes: Think of normalization not as a one-time task, but as a mindset. It asks: 'What facts are we storing? Which ones determine others? Where could inconsistency creep in?' Just as type systems prevent bugs in code, normalization prevents logical contradictions in data. In ML, this means your training data reflects reality—not accidental redundancy. Revisit it whenever the schema evolves.

slides.title: Key Takeaways on Database Normalization
bullets: Functional dependencies and closure identify candidate keys and redundancies
1NF requires atomic values; 2NF removes partial dependencies
3NF eliminates transitive dependencies; BCNF requires all determinants to be superkeys
Decomposition must balance normalization with dependency preservation
Denormalize only with safeguards—especially in ML feature stores
slides.speaker_notes: To summarize: normalization is a rigorous method to eliminate redundancy using functional dependencies. From 1NF to BCNF, each form targets a specific type of anomaly. While BCNF is ideal, it may not preserve all FDs. In practice, 3NF is often sufficient. In ML systems, always start normalized—then denormalize deliberately, with mechanisms to ensure consistency. Treat data design like software engineering: make dependencies explicit, testable, and maintainable.
